notes.title: Facts, dimensions, and grain
notes.body:
A fact table holds measurable events at a declared grain ('one row per order line'). Dimensions hold descriptive context (who/what/when/where). The grain statement is the most important sentence in modeling: every ambiguity in a dashboard traces back to an unstated grain.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Business process: online orders.
Grain: one row per order LINE ITEM (not per order: an order with 3 items
must be 3 rows, or item-level analysis is impossible).
Facts: quantity, unit_price, discount, net_amount (additive), order_id (degenerate dimension).
Dimensions: dim_date, dim_customer, dim_product, dim_promotion.
Test: 'Can I answer: revenue by product category by month?' Yes: join
facts to dim_product (category) and dim_date (month), sum net_amount.
If the grain were per-order, product-level questions would be unanswerable.
```

notes.title: Star vs snowflake
notes.body:
Star: denormalized dimensions (one dim_product with category columns). Snowflake: normalized dimensions (dim_product -> dim_category). Stars query simpler and faster (fewer joins); snowflakes save storage and enforce hierarchies. Modern warehouses favor stars — storage is cheap, analyst time is not.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Star: single join to get category revenue.
SELECT p.category, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_key = p.product_key
GROUP BY 1;
-- Snowflake equivalent needs two joins (product -> subcategory -> category).
-- Rule: snowflake only when a dimension hierarchy is maintained by a
-- separate team/system as its own master data; otherwise denormalize.
```

notes.title: Slowly changing dimensions: Types 1, 2, 3
notes.body:
Type 1: overwrite (no history — 'current address only'). Type 2: new row per change with effective dates + current flag (full history — 'show revenue by customer's region AT ORDER TIME'). Type 3: keep current + one previous value as columns (limited history). Choose by the question history must answer.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Type 2 dim_customer: same customer, two rows (one per address era).
-- customer_key | customer_id | region | eff_from   | eff_to     | is_current
-- 101          | 7           | West   | 2024-01-01 | 2026-03-14 | false
-- 102          | 7           | East   | 2026-03-15 | 9999-12-31 | true
-- Order on 2026-02-01 joins to key 101 (West): historical truth preserved.
-- Join condition: f.order_date BETWEEN d.eff_from AND d.eff_to.
-- Type 1 would have rewritten West->East and corrupted every historical report.
```

notes.title: The metrics layer: define once, use everywhere
notes.body:
A metrics layer (semantic model) defines each KPI once: its formula, grain, filters, and owner. Without it, five dashboards compute 'revenue' five ways. The layer sits between the warehouse and BI tools; every certified number comes from it.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
METRIC: net_revenue
  formula: SUM(fact_order_line.net_amount) WHERE status = 'paid'
  grain: order line; time spine: dim_date
  owner: Finance Analytics; certified: 2026-09-15
  includes: discounts, excludes: refunds (separate metric: refunds)
Governance rule: any dashboard titled with 'Revenue' must reference
net_revenue from the layer; custom calculations get a '_custom' suffix
and cannot be called 'revenue'.
```

notes.title: Warehouse design: denormalize deliberately
notes.body:
OLTP normalizes to prevent update anomalies; warehouses denormalize for read speed and analyst sanity. Pre-join, pre-aggregate, and use wide tables where the query pattern is known. Surrogate keys (integers) join faster and survive source-system key changes.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Wide daily mart: pre-joined, pre-aggregated for the dashboard's queries.
CREATE TABLE mart_daily_sales AS
SELECT d.date, p.category, c.region,
       SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue, COUNT(DISTINCT f.order_id) AS orders
FROM fact_order_line f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_key = p.product_key
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
-- The dashboard hits this 4-column mart, not 4 joins: fast and foolproof.
-- Surrogate keys (date_key, product_key) insulate the model from source
-- natural-key changes (e.g., product SKU renumbering).
```

notes.title: ETL vs ELT: where transformation lives
notes.body:
ETL: extract, transform (outside the warehouse), load. ELT: extract, load raw, transform inside the warehouse (dbt-style SQL). ELT wins when the warehouse is the strongest compute; ETL wins when transformation needs specialized engines (Spark) or must happen before landing for compliance.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Scenario: 'Nightly Salesforce + Postgres -> warehouse -> dbt models -> dashboard.'
Choice: ELT. Raw tables land untouched (audit trail + replayability),
dbt transforms version-controlled SQL inside the warehouse.
Scenario: 'PII must be masked before it ever lands in the lake.'
Choice: ETL (mask in transit): compliance forbids raw PII at rest.
Rule: default ELT for analytics; ETL when the LANDING ZONE has constraints
(compliance, specialized compute, or source-system offload).
```

notes.title: Idempotency: reruns must be safe
notes.body:
Pipelines fail and rerun. Idempotent = rerunning produces the same result as running once. Patterns: MERGE/upsert on business keys (not blind INSERT), date-partitioned overwrites (write the whole partition), watermark-based incremental loads, and dedup on (key, timestamp).

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Idempotent daily load: partition overwrite, not append.
-- Rerunning 2026-10-06 produces identical results (no duplicates).
DELETE FROM mart_daily WHERE date = '2026-10-06';  -- or partition overwrite
INSERT INTO mart_daily
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', order_at) AS date, region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM raw_orders
WHERE order_at >= '2026-10-06' AND order_at < '2026-10-07'
GROUP BY 1, 2;
-- Anti-pattern: blind INSERT ... SELECT rerun = doubled revenue.
-- Watermark: store max(order_at) processed; next run starts there.
```

notes.title: Data-quality gates in the pipeline
notes.body:
Quality checks belong INSIDE the DAG as tasks that fail the run: row-count bounds, null-rate thresholds, freshness (max timestamp recency), uniqueness of keys, and distribution checks (mean within N sigma of history). A failed check pages the owner; it never silently passes.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# dbt-style test block (conceptual; adapt to your orchestrator):
checks = [
    ('row_count', 'mart_daily', lambda df: 900 <= len(df) <= 1100),
    ('no_null_keys', 'mart_daily', lambda df: df['order_id'].notna().all()),
    ('freshness', 'raw_orders', lambda df: (now() - df['order_at'].max()).days < 2),
    ('revenue_sanity', 'mart_daily', lambda df: df['revenue'].sum() > 0),
]
# Each check is a DAG task AFTER the load, BEFORE downstream consumers.
# Failed check -> task fails -> downstream skipped -> alert fires.
# Never 'warn and continue' on a revenue table.
```

notes.title: Orchestration: DAGs, retries, SLAs, backfills
notes.body:
An orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect) schedules DAGs: tasks with dependencies, retries with backoff, SLAs, and alerting. Backfill reruns historical windows (for late data or bug fixes). Key analyst literacy: read a DAG, know what failed, and know whether a backfill is needed.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
DAG: extract_sales >> clean >> dbt_models >> quality_gates >> dashboard_refresh
Incident: clean failed at 03:00 (source schema added a column).
Analyst playbook:
1. Read the task log: which task, what error (schema mismatch, not data).
2. Fix the extraction (allow/rename the new column), NOT the dashboard.
3. Rerun from the failed task (downstream tasks rerun automatically).
4. If the bug corrupted 3 days of marts: backfill those 3 partitions
   (idempotent overwrite makes this safe), then verify quality gates.
Never backfill by hand-editing tables: rerun the DAG.
```

notes.title: Streaming vs batch: the latency/cost trade
notes.body:
Batch: simple, cheap, latent (hourly/daily). Micro-batch: minutes of latency, moderate complexity. Streaming: seconds, significant complexity (late data, watermarks, exactly-once). Choose the SLOWEST latency the business decision actually needs — most 'real-time dashboards' are fine hourly.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Three asks, three answers:
'Fraud alerts within seconds'      -> streaming (Flink/Kafka Streams),
                                         watermarks handle late events.
'Ops dashboard refreshed often'    -> micro-batch every 5-15 min (near-real-time
                                         feel, batch simplicity).
'Executive weekly revenue review'  -> daily batch. Anything faster burns money
                                         for zero decision value.
Challenge every 'real-time' request: 'What decision changes in the next
60 seconds vs the next 60 minutes?' The answer picks the architecture.
```

notes.title: Warehouses, lakes, lakehouses: the neutral map
notes.body:
Warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake/Redshift): structured analytics, strong governance, per-query or per-second compute pricing. Lake (S3/ADLS/GCS): cheap raw storage, open formats, weak native governance. Lakehouse (Delta/Iceberg/Hudi on lake storage): lake economics + ACID + schema enforcement. The workload picks the platform, not the logo.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Workload -> platform mapping:
'Finance needs governed, audited monthly close numbers' -> warehouse
  (governance + SQL maturity outweigh storage cost).
'10 PB of raw clickstream, ML + ad-hoc exploration' -> lake/lakehouse
  (open formats, cheap storage, Spark-native).
'One team, mixed BI + ML, wants one governed copy' -> lakehouse
  (single copy serving both engines).
Anti-pattern: choosing by vendor relationship, then discovering the
workload mismatch in production.
```

notes.title: How cloud data platforms bill you
notes.body:
Two meters: storage (per GB-month, cheap) and compute (per query byte scanned, per second, or per credit — expensive). Separation of compute and storage means idle compute costs nothing if you suspend it. The analyst's cost levers: scan less (partition, columnar), compute less (right-size, suspend), store colder (lifecycle tiers).

Worked example (with solution):
```text
A 5 TB table queried 20x/day, each query scanning everything:
scanned = 5 TB x 20 = 100 TB/day.
After partitioning by date + Parquet (10x scan reduction): 10 TB/day.
After clustering + only querying needed columns: ~2 TB/day.
Same answers, ~50x cheaper. The analyst controls the biggest cost lever
(query design), not the platform team.
Analyst rule: every new scheduled query gets a 'bytes per run' estimate
before it ships.
```

notes.title: File formats and partitioning: the physics
notes.body:
Row formats (CSV/JSON): human-readable, terrible for analytics. Columnar (Parquet/ORC): read only needed columns, compress 5-10x. Partitioning (by date/region): skip whole directories. Clustering/Z-order: colocate filtered values within files. These are the same physics on every cloud.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Partition pruning math: 3 years of daily data, query asks for last 7 days.
# Unpartitioned: scan 1,095 days of files.
# Partitioned by date: scan 7 directories -> ~150x less I/O.
# Columnar bonus: query needs 3 of 40 columns -> read ~1/13th of each file.
# Combined: three orders of magnitude less data touched.
# That is why 'partition by date, store as Parquet' is the first line of
# every cloud data platform runbook, vendor-neutrally.
```

notes.title: Build vs buy: BI and transformation tooling
notes.body:
Buy (managed BI, managed dbt Cloud, serverless warehouses): speed, support, per-seat/compute pricing. Build (open-source Superset/Metabase, self-hosted): control, lower license cost, higher ops burden. Total-cost reasoning includes the scarcest resource: your team's time.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
10-person analytics team choosing BI:
Buy: $70/user/month = $8.4K/yr + zero ops. Live in a week.
Build (self-hosted OSS): $0 licenses + ~0.5 FTE ops ($60K/yr loaded)
+ 6 weeks to production-grade.
Unless the team HAS spare ops capacity, buying wins on total cost.
The analyst's input: 'Which questions must the tool answer, and what does
switching cost us in retraining?' — not feature-matrix bingo.
```

notes.title: Vendor-neutral analyst skills that transfer
notes.body:
SQL dialects differ; the concepts don't: window functions, CTEs, and set logic work everywhere. Partitioning, columnar storage, and cost-aware querying transfer across all clouds. Governance (catalogs, lineage, access control) is a concept before it is a product.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Transfer checklist (new platform in week 1):
1. How are queries billed here? (per byte / per second / per credit)
2. Where is partitioning/clustering configured?
3. What is the columnar format story? (native? open?)
4. How do I see bytes-scanned per query? (the cost feedback loop)
5. Where do access grants live? (who can see what)
Answer these five and you are productive on ANY platform in days.
A platform-specific certification tests the same five in vendor vocabulary.
```

notes.title: Chart choice: the question names the chart
notes.body:
Trend over time -> line. Comparison across categories -> bar (sorted). Part of whole (few parts) -> stacked bar. Distribution -> histogram. Relationship -> scatter. Never start with the chart; start with the question, then the chart is forced.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Question-to-chart mapping drill:
'Are sales growing?'                    -> line (trend)
'Which region sells most?'              -> sorted bar (comparison)
'What share is each channel?'           -> stacked bar, few channels (composition)
'How are order values distributed?'      -> histogram (distribution)
'Do discounts lift units?'               -> scatter + trend (relationship)
Exam/interview trap: 'show monthly revenue AND order count' -> NOT a dual-axis
line by default; two aligned panels avoid the dual-axis distortion trap.
```

notes.title: Dashboard design: takeaways, filters, comparisons
notes.body:
Every dashboard answers one decision. Titles state takeaways ('Churn concentrates in month 2'), not topics. Filters apply consistently or say why not. Every visual carries comparison context: prior period, target, or benchmark — a number without comparison is trivia.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Bad: 'Q3 Sales' dashboard, 12 unsorted charts, no targets, filters affect
some sheets, pie with 9 slices.
Rebuild:
1. Title: 'Q3 missed plan by 4%; the West region is the gap.'
2. Three KPI tiles: revenue vs target, orders vs target, AOV vs target.
3. One trend (actual vs target line), one sorted bar (gap by region).
4. Filters (date, region) apply to ALL sheets; stated in the subtitle.
5. Pie replaced by stacked bar (9 slices are unreadable as angles).
Same data, opposite usefulness.
```

notes.title: Perception: preattentive attributes and color
notes.body:
Preattentive attributes (position, length, color intensity) are decoded instantly; angles and areas are decoded poorly (hence: bars over pies, position over color). Color discipline: one hue ramp per metric, color for meaning (alerts, categories), never decoration. Red/green needs a non-color redundant cue for colorblind viewers.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Redesigning a 'traffic light' KPI table:
Bad: 40 cells colored red/yellow/green, no numbers visible.
Good: numbers first (the value IS the message), with a single ▲/▼/● marker
and muted color as reinforcement — readable in grayscale, honest about
magnitude (a 'red' -0.2% and a 'red' -40% are very different stories).
Rule: if the chart fails in grayscale, color was carrying meaning it shouldn't.
```

notes.title: Axis honesty and the lie detector
notes.body:
Truncated y-axes exaggerate change; dual axes invite false correlation; 3D distorts values; area encodes quadratically (a 2x value looks 4x). The analyst's lie detector: ask 'what would this look like at zero baseline and single axis?' before publishing.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# The truncated-axis exaggeration, quantified:
import numpy as np
vals = np.array([98, 100, 102])
# Full axis 0-110: bars nearly identical (truth: +-2% noise).
# Truncated axis 95-105: middle bar looks 2x the first (lie: 100 vs 98
# rendered as double height because (100-95)/(98-95) = 5/3).
# Rule: bar charts start at zero (length encodes value); line charts may
# zoom ONLY with an explicit annotation ('y-axis starts at 95').
print('bar height ratio on 95-105 axis:', (100-95)/(98-95))  # 1.67x for a 2% diff
```

notes.title: Storytelling: the 3-minute dashboard walkthrough
notes.body:
Present dashboards as stories: context (the decision), complication (what changed), resolution (what we recommend). The 3-minute version: one takeaway per visual, in logical order, ending with the ask. Stakeholders remember narratives, not charts.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
3-minute walkthrough script:
0:00 'Decision: should we expand the loyalty program?' (the ask, first)
0:30 'Members retain 2x better...' (the headline visual)
1:00 '...but the lift concentrates in tenured users' (the Simpson check)
1:30 'Cost per retained member: $18 vs $41 for discount campaigns' (the economics)
2:00 'Risk: novelty effect; recommend a 90-day holdout before full rollout' (honesty)
2:30 'Ask: approve the holdout test.' (close the loop)
Structure beats polish: a plain deck with this arc outperforms a beautiful
dashboard with no narrative.
```

notes.title: Logical formulas: IFS, SWITCH, and nested logic done right
notes.body:
IFS tests conditions in order and returns the first match; SWITCH matches exact values; nested IFs work but rot quickly. Guard every logical formula with a catch-all (TRUE as the last IFS condition) so unexpected inputs can't slip through silently.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Risk tier from days-overdue in D2:
=IFS(D2=0, "Current", D2<=30, "Watch", D2<=60, "Elevated", D2<=90, "High", TRUE, "Critical")
Order matters: D2=45 hits D2<=60 before D2<=90. The TRUE catch-all
catches negatives and text (data errors become 'Critical' -> visible,
not silently blank).
SWITCH for exact codes: =SWITCH(C2, "W","West", "E","East", "N","North", "S","South", "Unknown")
Audit rule: any logical formula without a catch-all is a bug waiting for
the one input you didn't imagine.
```

notes.title: Lookups: XLOOKUP and INDEX-MATCH
notes.body:
XLOOKUP(value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found]) searches in any direction with exact match by default. INDEX-MATCH is the legacy flexible combo. Absolute-reference the arrays ($A$2:$A$100) so formulas copy safely down columns.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Price lookup: product code in B2, price table codes in $F$2:$F$500,
prices in $G$2:$G$500:
=XLOOKUP(B2, $F$2:$F$500, $G$2:$G$500, "NOT FOUND") * C2
The "NOT FOUND" fourth argument turns missing codes into visible errors
instead of #N/A cascades. Multiply by quantity C2 inline.
Two-column return (price AND category):
=XLOOKUP(B2, $F$2:$F$500, $G$2:$H$500, "NOT FOUND")  -- spills both columns
INDEX-MATCH equivalent: =INDEX($G$2:$G$500, MATCH(B2, $F$2:$F$500, 0))
```

notes.title: Pivot tables: ad-hoc analysis in minutes
notes.body:
Pivot tables are GROUP BY with a GUI: rows/columns/filters/values. Add slicers for stakeholder-friendly filtering, use 'Show Values As' (% of total, running total, difference from), and refresh discipline (data changes -> refresh, or the pivot lies).

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Question: 'Which sales rep beats target most consistently by quarter?'
Pivot: Rows=Rep, Columns=Quarter, Values=SUM(Revenue) AND SUM(Target),
then a calculated field = SUM(Revenue)/SUM(Target) formatted as %.
'Show Values As -> % Difference From -> Previous Quarter' reveals momentum.
Slicer on Region lets the stakeholder self-serve.
Trap: pivots cache data. After the source updates, RIGHT-CLICK -> Refresh
(or the numbers are stale and nobody tells you).
```

notes.title: Power Query: cleaning you can rerun
notes.body:
Power Query (Get & Transform) records every cleaning step as re-runnable M code: split columns, unpivot, fix types, merge queries, fill down. The month-end report becomes 'Refresh All' instead of a morning of manual fixes.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Monthly CSV arrives with: dates as text 'Jan-2026', amounts with '$' and
commas, region in merged header cells.
Power Query steps:
1. Promote headers; fill down region (merged cells).
2. Replace '$' and ',' in amount; change type to Decimal.
3. Parse date text to Date type.
4. Unpivot the 12 month columns into (Month, Value) rows.
Save as the month-end template: next month, drop in the new CSV and
Refresh. Manual cleaning time: 2 hours -> 2 minutes, and auditable.
```

notes.title: Model design: inputs, calcs, outputs, checks
notes.body:
Professional models separate: INPUTS (assumptions, blue cells), CALCULATIONS (formulas only), OUTPUTS (results/charts), CHECKS (balance/error tests). No hard-coded numbers inside formulas — every assumption lives in INPUTS and is referenced.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Forecast model layout:
[Inputs]      Growth rate: 8% (B2, blue) | Churn: 3% (B3, blue)
[Calcs]       =B2-B3 for net growth; revenue_t+1 = revenue_t*(1+net)
[Outputs]     12-month revenue table + chart
[Checks]     =IF(SUM(checks)<>0,"ERROR","OK"): e.g., customer count
              continuity (start + adds - churns = end), no negative revenue.
Hard-coded sin: =100000*1.08^12 (where did 8% come from? unauditable).
Virtue: =B5*(1+$B$2)^12 (assumption visible, changeable, documented).
```

cards.back: TRUE as the last condition: =IFS(..., TRUE, "fallback").
if_not_found: turns missing keys into visible text instead of #N/A cascades.
So the range doesn't shift when the formula copies down.
% of total, running total, difference from previous — built-in comparative views.

objectives: Apply data-privacy fundamentals (PII identification, minimization, masking, retention) to analyst workflows.
Explain GDPR/CCPA-style rights (access, deletion, opt-out) at the level an analyst needs for compliant analysis.
Design ethical analyses: consent, fairness checks, and honest communication of uncertainty and limits.
Build governance habits: data dictionaries, lineage notes, access justification, and audit-ready documentation.

notes.title: PII: find it, minimize it, mask it
notes.body:
PII = data identifying a person (name, email, SSN, device IDs, precise location). Quasi-identifiers (ZIP + birthdate + gender) re-identify when combined. Analyst rules: collect the minimum, mask in extracts (hash/tokenize/last-4), never email raw PII, and set retention/expiry on every extract.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Safe analyst extract: hash the email (joinable but not readable),
# keep only last-4 of phone, drop exact address for ZIP.
import hashlib
def tokenize(v): return hashlib.sha256(v.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
# email -> tokenize(email); phone -> '***-***-' + phone[-4:]; address -> zip only
# The extract answers the churn question WITHOUT exposing identities.
# Document: purpose, columns, masking applied, expiry date, approver.
# Rule: if the analysis doesn't need the identifier, it doesn't ship.
```

notes.title: Privacy rights an analyst must respect
notes.body:
Modern privacy regimes grant: right to access (see my data), deletion/erasure, opt-out of sale/sharing, and data portability. For analysts this means: honor deletion requests across marts (not just the source), respect opt-out flags in every audience build, and never re-identify anonymized data.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Deletion request arrives for user 48291.
Checklist:
1. Source systems: delete/anonymize per policy.
2. Warehouse marts: rebuild affected partitions (Type-2 dims, aggregates).
3. Extracts: expire/purge any analyst CSVs containing the user.
4. Backups: covered by retention policy (documented, not instant).
5. ML features: retrain or document exclusion.
The analyst's job: know WHERE the user's data lives (lineage) and confirm
each copy's disposition. 'Deleted from prod' is not 'deleted everywhere'.
```

notes.title: Fairness: check your models and metrics for bias
notes.body:
Analyses can encode bias: training on historical decisions bakes in past discrimination; proxies (ZIP code for race) sneak past removed attributes. Fairness checks: compare error rates and outcomes across groups, test with/without suspect features, and document limitations.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Fairness audit: approval rates by group for a lead-scoring model.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'group': ['A','A','B','B'],
    'approved': [82, 78, 61, 59],  # per 100 applicants, two periods
    'applicants': [100, 100, 100, 100]})
rates = df.groupby('group')['approved'].mean()
print(rates)  # A: 80.0, B: 60.0 -> 20-point gap demands investigation
# Next: check whether the gap persists after controlling for legitimate
# risk factors; if it does, the model (or the process) needs remediation.
# Document the audit: method, finding, action. Silence is the failure mode.
```

notes.title: Ethics of communication: uncertainty and limits
notes.body:
Ethical analysis communication: state uncertainty (CIs, not point estimates), disclose limits (what the data cannot say), correct misreadings even when inconvenient, and never cherry-pick. The analyst's credibility is the product.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Dishonest: 'The campaign lifted conversion 25%!' (relative %, no CI, no caveats).
Honest: 'Conversion rose from 4.0% to 5.0% (+1.0pp, 95% CI +0.2 to +1.8).
The test ran 2 weeks; novelty effects may inflate early results. The lift
is significant but the lower bound is small: recommend a 4-week holdout
before full rollout.'
Same data. One version informs a decision; the other manufactures one.
Ethics is a communication discipline, not just a data-handling one.
```

notes.title: Governance habits: dictionaries, lineage, access
notes.body:
Governance for analysts = boring excellence: a data dictionary for every mart (definitions, owners, refresh cadence), lineage notes (where each column came from), access justification (why you have it), and versioned analysis code. Audits are easy when the paperwork already exists.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Data dictionary entry (the minimum viable governance):
  table: mart_daily_revenue
  owner: Analytics Eng | refresh: daily 06:00 ET | SLA: 09:00 ET
  grain: one row per date x region
  columns:
    date        DATE        'Transaction date (ET)'
    region      VARCHAR     'Sales region, standardized list'
    revenue     DECIMAL     'Net paid revenue USD; excludes refunds'
  lineage: raw_orders -> stg_orders (dbt) -> mart_daily_revenue
  access: analysts role (SELECT); no PII columns present
Write this BEFORE the dashboard, not during the audit.
```

cards.back: PII directly identifies; quasi-identifiers (ZIP+birthdate+gender) re-identify in combination.
Minimize, mask (hash/tokenize/last-4), never email raw, set extract expiry.
Source, marts (rebuild partitions), extracts (purge), backups (retention policy), ML features.
Outcome/error rates by group; investigate gaps, test without suspect features.
Honest: effect + CI + limits + recommendation. Dishonest: bare relative %.
Owner, refresh/SLA, grain, column definitions, lineage, access.
ZIP code standing in for race after removing the race column.
Marts, extracts, and features still hold copies — disposition each via lineage.

choices: Grain + column definitions with business meaning

objectives: Run stakeholder discovery: extract the real decision, deadline, and definition of done before touching data.
Manage expectations with written confirmations, interim updates, and honest renegotiation when scope or data slips.
Present findings in pyramid structure (answer first), tailored to executive vs technical audiences.
Handle difficult dynamics: moving goalposts, data disputes, and 'just get me the number' pressure without caving.

notes.title: Discovery: the 15 minutes that save 15 hours
notes.body:
Every request gets discovery before data: What decision will this inform? By when? What does 'done' look like? Which metric definition? What will you do if the answer is X vs Y? The stakeholder who can't answer is telling you the request isn't real yet.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Request: 'Can you pull churn numbers?'
Discovery (5 questions, 15 minutes):
1. Decision: 'We're deciding whether to fund the win-back campaign.'
2. Deadline: 'Board deck Friday.'
3. Definition: 'Logo churn or revenue churn? Which date range?'
4. Done looks like: 'One slide: churn by cohort with the campaign breakeven.'
5. If X vs Y: 'If churn > 8%, we fund; under 5%, we kill it.'
Result: a scoped, decision-shaped deliverable instead of a 'churn numbers'
swamp. Send the written confirmation email before starting.
```

notes.title: Written confirmations and expectation management
notes.body:
After discovery, send the confirmation: decision, deadline, definitions, deliverable, and caveats. Interim updates ('on track, found a data gap in X, still Friday') prevent surprise slips. When scope creeps, renegotiate explicitly: 'I can add Y if we move the deadline to Tuesday or drop Z.'

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Confirmation email template:
Subject: Confirming: churn analysis for win-back decision (due Fri)
- Decision: fund/kill win-back campaign
- Metric: logo churn, monthly cohorts, Jan-Jun 2026
- Deliverable: one slide + appendix, by Fri 2pm
- Caveat: March data has a tracking gap (noted in appendix)
- If blocked: I'll flag by Wed noon with options
This email IS the contract. Scope changes arrive as replies to it,
not as hallway ambushes.
```

notes.title: Pyramid presentations: answer first
notes.body:
Pyramid principle: lead with the answer, then the supporting arguments, then the data. Executives get the one-slide version; technical audiences get the appendix. Never open with methodology — it buries the decision.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Bad opening: 'We pulled data from three sources, cleaned it with...' (eyes glaze).
Pyramid opening:
'RECOMMENDATION: Fund the win-back campaign.
 - Churn is 9.2%, above the 8% funding threshold.
 - Win-back converts 22% of churned logos at $41 CAC vs $120 new-logo CAC.
 - Risk: March tracking gap; sensitivity analysis holds above 8% regardless.'
Then: the one chart. Then: 'Details in the appendix.'
The executive decides in 60 seconds; the analyst's rigor lives underneath.
```

notes.title: 'Just get me the number': holding the line kindly
notes.body:
Pressure for a fast number without definitions is how bad decisions get made. The senior move: deliver a fast DIRECTIONAL answer with written caveats, while the rigorous version runs. Never let a caveat-free number leave your hands.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
'Board needs the number in an hour!'
Response: 'I'll send a directional estimate by 3pm with caveats in writing;
the audited number follows tomorrow 10am. The estimate uses [definition];
it excludes [segment] because that table isn't refreshed yet.'
Send BOTH the number AND the caveats in the same message (caveats in a
separate doc get separated from the number in forwarding).
What you never do: silently ship the quick number as final. That number
will outlive your caveats in every forwarded deck.
```

notes.title: Disputes and moving goalposts
notes.body:
Data disputes: reproduce their number first (you'll often find the definition difference), then reconcile definitions in writing. Moving goalposts: name it kindly ('This is a new question — I'll scope it separately'), and protect the original deliverable's deadline.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
'Your churn number doesn't match Finance's!'
Playbook:
1. Reproduce Finance's number exactly (find their definition).
2. Typical finding: Finance uses revenue churn, you used logo churn.
3. Write the reconciliation: 'Finance 6.1% (revenue), Analytics 9.2% (logo).
   Both correct under their definitions. Recommend: report both, label clearly.'
4. Add both to the metrics layer so the dispute never recurs.
You win disputes by reproducing, not by arguing. Definitions end them.
```

cards.back: Decision? Deadline? Definition? Done-looks-like? If X vs Y?
Decision, deadline, definitions, deliverable, caveats — the contract.
Answer first, then supporting arguments, then data.
Directional estimate WITH written caveats now; audited number later. Never a caveat-free number.
Reproduce their number, find the definition difference, reconcile in writing, add to metrics layer.
Name it kindly; scope the new question separately; protect the original deadline.

cards.front: Why send caveats WITH the number?
cards.back: Caveats in a separate doc get separated in forwarding; the number outlives them.
Surprise slips: 'on track / found gap X / still Friday' beats silence.

notes.title: dplyr: the five verbs
notes.body:
filter() keeps rows, select() keeps columns, mutate() creates columns, summarise() aggregates (usually after group_by()), arrange() sorts. Piped with %>%, they read like sentences. This is the R half of the bilingual analyst.

Worked example (with solution):
```r
library(dplyr)
result <- orders %>%
  filter(status == "paid") %>%
  mutate(net = amount - discount,
         month = format(order_date, "%Y-%m")) %>%
  group_by(region, month) %>%
  summarise(revenue = sum(net),
            orders = n_distinct(order_id),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(region, month)
# n_distinct (not n()) avoids double-counting line items as orders:
# the same dplyr/pandas discipline in both languages.
```

notes.title: Joins and reshaping in R
notes.body:
left_join/right_join/inner_join/full_join by a key; pivot_wider spreads long to wide; pivot_longer gathers wide to long. Join validation: check for duplicated keys before merging, or metrics fan out exactly as in pandas.

Worked example (with solution):
```r
library(tidyr)
# Key check BEFORE the join (the fan-out guard):
any(duplicated(customers$customer_id))  # must be FALSE for many-to-one
m <- orders %>% left_join(customers, by = "customer_id")
# Wide monthly columns -> long tidy rows:
long <- monthly_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("m_"),
               names_to = "month", values_to = "revenue")
```

notes.title: ggplot2: layered grammar
notes.body:
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_*(...) + labs(...): data, aesthetics (mappings), geometries (marks), then labels/scales/themes. Build plots additively; every layer is inspectable. Facets (facet_wrap) multiply a chart across groups — the small-multiple superpower.

Worked example (with solution):
```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = revenue, color = region, group = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(title = "Revenue trend by region",
       subtitle = "Takeaway: West recovers in Q3 while East plateaus",
       x = NULL, y = "Revenue ($K)") +
  theme_minimal()
# Subtitle carries the takeaway (the dashboard title rule, in R).
# facet_wrap gives small multiples: comparisons without overplotting.
```

notes.title: RMarkdown: reproducible reporting
notes.body:
RMarkdown interleaves narrative, code chunks, and output; knitting renders the report with fresh results every time. Set echo=FALSE for stakeholder versions (output without code), keep code visible for technical review. Reproducibility: set.seed() for randomness, relative paths, sessionInfo() recorded.

Worked example (with solution):
```r
# Report chunk pattern:
# ```{r monthly-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, message=FALSE}
# ggplot(monthly, aes(month, revenue)) + geom_col() +
#   labs(title = "Monthly revenue")
# ```
# Knit -> HTML/PDF with the chart embedded, computed from current data.
# Stakeholder version: echo=FALSE hides code. Technical appendix: echo=TRUE.
# set.seed(42) before any sampling/simulation for exact reproducibility.
```

notes.title: Bilingual: dplyr <-> pandas translation
notes.body:
Every dplyr verb has a pandas twin: filter->boolean mask, select->[[]], mutate->assign, summarise->agg, arrange->sort_values, group_by->groupby, left_join->merge. Learning the map doubles your employability and lets you verify results across languages.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
dplyr                              pandas
filter(status=="paid")            df[df.status=="paid"]
select(region, revenue)            df[["region","revenue"]]
mutate(net = amount-discount)      df.assign(net=df.amount-df.discount)
group_by(region) %>% summarise()    df.groupby("region").agg(...)
arrange(desc(revenue))             df.sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
left_join(customers, by="id")     df.merge(customers, on="id", how="left")
Verification habit: compute a KPI in both; they must match to the cent.
```

cards.back: filter, select, mutate, summarise, arrange.
n() counts rows; n_distinct counts unique orders (no line-item double count).
any(duplicated(key)) must be FALSE before a many-to-one join.
data + aesthetics + geometries + labels/scales/themes.
Small multiples: one chart panel per group.
Hides code, shows output — the stakeholder version.
assign().
merge(..., how='left').

objectives: Write interview-grade SQL under time pressure: window functions, CTEs, and complex joins with correct first-pass logic.
Narrate your SQL thinking aloud: state assumptions, grain, and edge cases before writing.
Handle follow-ups: optimize a working query, explain the plan, and adapt to schema twists.
Avoid the classic interview traps: fan-out, NULL semantics, duplicate keys, and off-by-one date logic.

notes.title: Thinking aloud: the interview meta-skill
notes.body:
Interviewers score reasoning, not just results. Narrate: restate the question, state the grain ('one row per user per day'), name edge cases (NULLs, duplicates, ties), then write. A correct query with silent assumptions scores lower than a good query with stated assumptions.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Q: 'Daily active users for the last 30 days.'
Aloud: 'DAU = distinct users with an event per day. Grain: one row per
user per day. Edge cases: duplicate events (dedupe by user+day), timezone
(events stored UTC, business day is ET), bots (exclude flagged accounts).
I'll assume the events table has user_id, event_at, is_bot.'
Then write:
SELECT DATE(CONVERT_TZ(event_at,'UTC','America/New_York')) AS day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau
FROM events
WHERE event_at >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 30 DAY AND NOT is_bot
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
The narration IS the senior signal.
```
Independent prep material; no affiliation with or endorsement by Palantir.

notes.title: Window functions under pressure
notes.body:
The interview core: rank per group, running totals, period-over-period, top-N with ties. Write the PARTITION BY first (it names the grouping), then the ORDER BY, then the frame. Say which rank function and why before writing it.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- 'Second purchase date per customer, and days between first and second.'
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT o1.customer_id, o1.order_date AS first_order,
       o2.order_date AS second_order,
       DATEDIFF(o2.order_date, o1.order_date) AS days_between
FROM ordered o1
JOIN ordered o2 ON o1.customer_id = o2.customer_id
  AND o1.rn = 1 AND o2.rn = 2;
-- Aloud: 'ROW_NUMBER (not RANK) because I need exactly the 1st and 2nd
-- rows; ties broken arbitrarily by order_date, which I'll state.'
```

notes.title: Joins, fan-out, and NULL traps live
notes.body:
Under pressure, joins break two ways: fan-out (duplicated keys multiply rows) and NULL keys (dropped by inner joins). State the key-uniqueness assumption before joining; use LEFT JOIN deliberately; never NOT IN with nullable subqueries.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- 'Customers with no orders in 2026.'
-- Trap answer: WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders ...)
--   breaks if any order.customer_id is NULL.
-- Senior answer:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2027-01-01'
);
-- Aloud: 'NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe; NOT IN is not. I'm also scoping the
-- date range explicitly rather than YEAR() so an index stays usable.'
```

notes.title: Date logic without off-by-ones
notes.body:
Half-open intervals [start, end) prevent double-counting and gaps: >= first-day AND < first-of-next. Never YEAR(x)=2026 on indexed columns; never BETWEEN with timestamps (end-of-day gaps). State the timezone.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- 'Revenue by month for 2026, no gaps, no double counts.'
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- Aloud: 'Half-open interval: includes Jan 1 00:00, excludes Jan 1 2027
-- 00:00. BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31' would MISS Dec 31 afternoon
-- timestamps. This is the off-by-one interviewers hunt for.'
```

notes.title: Follow-ups: optimize and adapt
notes.body:
After a working query, expect: 'Make it faster' (index the filter/join columns, avoid the sort), 'What if the schema changes?' (adapt the grain), 'How do you test it?' (row-count reconciliation, spot checks, edge-case rows). Answer structurally, not defensively.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Follow-up: 'This runs on 500M rows. Make it faster.'
Answer aloud: 'First, check the plan for a full scan: the selective filter
is on status, so I'd index (status, order_date). Second, the GROUP BY sorts
500M rows: pre-aggregate to a daily mart if this query runs often.
Third, confirm stats are fresh (ANALYZE) so the planner picks hash join.
I'd verify with EXPLAIN before and after.'
Follow-up: 'How do you know it's right?' -> 'Reconcile: total revenue
matches the finance mart; spot-check 5 customers by hand; test NULL
and duplicate edge cases explicitly.'
```

notes.title: Probability under pressure: the interview toolkit
notes.body:
Interview probability questions reward structured counting: define the sample space, count favorable outcomes, and narrate. Bayes for 'given that' inversions; expectation for decision questions; complements for 'at least one'.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Q: 'A test is 95% accurate; 1% of users have the condition. Positive result:
probability of actually having it?'
Aloud: 'Bayes. P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / P(+). P(+) = 0.95*0.01 + 0.05*0.99.'
Numerator: 0.95 * 0.01 = 0.0095.
Denominator: 0.0095 + 0.05*0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059.
Answer: 0.0095/0.059 = 0.161 -> 16%.
Closer: 'So 84% of positives are false alarms: the base rate dominates.'
The closer (business implication) is what separates senior answers.
```
Independent prep material; no affiliation with or endorsement by Palantir.

notes.title: Python/pandas live: wrangle and narrate
notes.body:
Live coding tests idiomatic pandas: groupby, merge, window-equivalents (shift, cumsum, rank), and string/datetime handling. Narrate the shape at each step ('now one row per user per day'). Avoid loops; know vectorized alternatives.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# 'For each user, days between signup and first purchase (null if never).'
import pandas as pd
users = pd.DataFrame({'user_id':[1,2,3], 'signup':pd.to_datetime(['2026-01-01','2026-01-05','2026-01-10'])})
orders = pd.DataFrame({'user_id':[1,1,3], 'order_date':pd.to_datetime(['2026-01-03','2026-01-09','2026-01-10'])})
first = orders.groupby('user_id')['order_date'].min().rename('first_order')
out = users.merge(first, on='user_id', how='left')
out['days_to_first'] = (out['first_order'] - out['signup']).dt.days
print(out[['user_id','days_to_first']])
# user 1: 2 days; user 2: NaN (never purchased); user 3: 0 days.
# Aloud: 'left join keeps non-buyers as NaN; min() takes the FIRST order.'
```

notes.title: Product sense: metrics and trade-offs
notes.body:
Product-sense questions ('How would you measure success for X?') want: the goal, 2-3 key metrics (one north star + guards), segment cuts, and trade-off discussion. Structure: clarify goal -> propose metrics -> discuss gaming/risks -> experiment design.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Q: 'How would you measure a new onboarding flow?'
'Goal: activate new users faster without hurting quality.
North star: activation rate (key action within 7 days).
Guards: Day-30 retention (no junk activations), support tickets/user.
Segments: by acquisition channel and device (effects differ).
Gaming risk: teams could lower the 'activation' bar; define it as the
  action correlated with retention, not any click.
Experiment: randomized rollout, 2-week minimum (novelty), pre-registered
  primary = activation, guards as veto metrics.'
Structure + trade-offs + experiment = the complete answer.
```

notes.title: Estimation: Fermi reasoning that lands
notes.body:
Estimation questions test structured decomposition, not accuracy: break into countable pieces, state assumptions, multiply, sanity-check. Round aggressively; the structure is graded.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Q: 'How many queries does a data warehouse run per day at a mid-size company?'
'50 analysts. Each runs ~20 queries/day (ad-hoc + refreshes) = 1,000.
Scheduled pipelines: 200 DAGs x 5 queries = 1,000.
Dashboards: 100 dashboards x 10 tiles x 4 refreshes = 4,000.
Total ~6,000/day. Sanity: that is ~4/minute average, spiky at 9am:
plausible for mid-size. I'd state the three buckets explicitly so the
interviewer can correct any assumption.'
Buckets + assumptions + sanity check = full marks.
```

notes.title: Behavioral: STAR with data quantified
notes.body:
Behavioral rounds want STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) with quantified data impact. Prepare 5 stories: disagreement with a stakeholder, a wrong analysis you caught, an experiment that failed, a metric you defined, mentoring. Each ends with a number.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
' Tell me about a time your analysis changed a decision.'
S: 'Marketing planned to cut the affiliate channel (low last-click revenue).'
T: 'I was asked to validate the cut.'
A: 'I ran a multi-touch attribution check and found affiliates ASSISTED
   31% of enterprise deals that closed via direct.'
R: 'The cut was reversed; affiliate spend was reallocated not removed.
   Sourced pipeline from affiliates: $2.1M the next quarter.'
The number ($2.1M) makes it memorable; the method (attribution check)
makes it credible.
```

objectives: Explain ontology thinking: entities, relationships, and properties as the shared language between business and data.
Map a business domain to an ontology: identify objects, links, and the questions each link answers.
Design pipelines with ontology discipline: raw -> cleaned -> modeled (ontology objects) -> served, with contracts at each boundary.
Evaluate build-vs-buy and data-quality trade-offs through the ontology lens: which objects must be first-class.

notes.title: Ontology: the shared map of the business
notes.body:
An ontology names the business's objects (Customer, Order, Shipment), their properties, and their links (Customer PLACED Order; Order CONTAINS Product). It is the contract between stakeholders ('what we mean') and data ('what we store'). Without it, every team defines 'customer' differently.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
E-commerce ontology (fragment):
Objects: Customer, Order, LineItem, Product, Shipment, Return.
Links: Customer PLACED Order (1:many); Order HAS LineItem (1:many);
       LineItem REFERENCES Product (many:1); Order FULFILLED_BY Shipment;
       Return AGAINST LineItem.
Questions each link answers:
  PLACED -> 'orders per customer' (the join path)
  REFERENCES -> 'revenue by product' (the attribution path)
  AGAINST -> 'return rate by product' (the quality path)
If a question has no link path, the ontology (not the query) is missing it.
```
Independent prep material; no affiliation with or endorsement by Palantir.

notes.title: From ontology to schema
notes.body:
Ontology objects become tables (or nodes); links become foreign keys (or edges); properties become columns. The discipline: every table maps to an ontology object, every join follows an ontology link. Mystery joins (paths with no business meaning) are a modeling smell.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Ontology-driven schema: each table IS an ontology object.
CREATE TABLE customer (customer_id PK, name, segment, ...);       -- Object
CREATE TABLE "order" (order_id PK, customer_id FK -> customer, ...); -- Object + link
CREATE TABLE line_item (line_id PK, order_id FK -> "order",
                         product_id FK -> product, qty, price);     -- Object + 2 links
-- The join customer -> order -> line_item -> product FOLLOWS the ontology.
-- Anti-pattern: joining customer straight to shipment with no link in the
-- ontology ('which shipments belong to which customer?') -> add the link
-- (Shipment FULFILLS Order) instead of hacking the join.
```

notes.title: Pipeline thinking: contracts at every boundary
notes.body:
Production pipelines are staged: raw (immutable landings) -> cleaned (typed, deduped) -> modeled (ontology objects) -> served (marts/APIs). Each boundary has a contract: schema, freshness SLA, quality gates. Breaks are diagnosed at boundaries, not in the middle of a 500-line query.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Pipeline: raw_events -> stg_events -> fct_orders -> mart_daily
Contracts:
  raw_events:     append-only, any schema (quarantined on violation)
  stg_events:     typed, deduped on event_id, <2h freshness
  fct_orders:     one row per order (grain!), FKs valid, quality gates pass
  mart_daily:     matches fct_orders totals (reconciliation gate)
Incident: mart_daily revenue dropped 30%.
Diagnose at boundaries: mart==fct? fct==stg? stg==raw? The FIRST boundary
where numbers diverge names the broken stage. No guessing.
```

notes.title: Ontology in interviews: the modeling case
notes.body:
Ontology-style interview cases ('design data for a ride-share app') are won by: naming objects/links first, stating grain per object, then sketching the schema. The interviewer watches whether the model follows the business or the business follows the model.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
' Design analytics for ride-share.'
Objects: Rider, Driver, Trip, Payment, Rating.
Links: Rider REQUESTED Trip; Driver ACCEPTED Trip; Trip HAS Payment;
       Rider RATED Driver; Driver RATED Rider.
Grain: Trip = one row per completed ride attempt (cancelled = status).
Key questions -> paths:
  'Driver utilization' -> ACCEPTED links per driver per hour.
  'Cancellation rate'  -> Trip.status distribution.
  'Take rate'          -> Payment.driver_payout vs rider_fare.
Then schema. The ontology did the hard thinking; SQL is transcription.
```

notes.title: Data quality through the ontology lens
notes.body:
Ontology discipline makes quality concrete: every object needs identity (unique keys), every link needs referential integrity, every property needs a type and allowed values. Orphaned links (orders with no customer) and identity breaks (duplicated keys) are ontology violations with business meaning.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Ontology-driven quality checks (each maps to a link/identity rule):
-- 1. Identity: no duplicated order_id
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- 2. Link integrity: no orphan line items
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM line_item l
LEFT JOIN "order" o ON l.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
-- 3. Property validity: quantities positive
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM line_item WHERE qty <= 0;
-- Each check has a BUSINESS reading: orphans = lost attribution;
-- dup keys = double-counted revenue. Quality is ontology enforcement.
```

Check each boundary in order; the first divergence names the broken stage.
Rider, Driver, Trip, Payment, Rating (+ links: requested/accepted/has/rated).
A join with no ontology link: a modeling smell; add the link instead.
Identity (unique keys), link integrity (no orphans), property validity.

notes.title: Banking data domains: the map
notes.body:
A bank's data splits into domains: Deposits (accounts, balances, transactions), Lending (loans, delinquency, provisions), Payments (wires, ACH, cards, settlement), Custody/Asset Servicing (holdings, corporate actions, NAV), Markets (trades, positions, risk). Each has its own systems, clocks, and definitions of 'the truth'.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
'Where did yesterday's $2M wire go?' -> trace across domains:
Payments: wire instruction (sender, receiver, amount, status=settled).
Deposits: sender account debited, receiver account credited (double-entry).
GL: the bank's books balance (debits = credits).
If Payments says 'settled' but Deposits shows no credit: a reconciliation
BREAK — the core banking-data failure mode. Analysts live in these breaks.
```
Independent prep material; no affiliation with or endorsement by BNY Mellon.

notes.title: Double-entry and the GL: the bank's source of truth
notes.body:
Every financial event posts balanced debits and credits to the General Ledger. Subledgers (loan system, deposit system) must reconcile to the GL. 'Reconciled to the GL' is the banking equivalent of 'tests pass' — nothing ships unaudited against it.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Wire of $2M from A to B posts:
  Dr Customer A deposit liability  $2,000,000
  Cr Cash / settlement account    $2,000,000   (sender leg)
  Dr Cash / settlement account    $2,000,000
  Cr Customer B deposit liability $2,000,000   (receiver leg)
Four balanced lines. If the subledger sum differs from the GL by $1:
STOP. Find the break (timing? fee? failed post?) before any reporting.
Analyst rule: never present subledger numbers that don't tie to the GL.
```

notes.title: Reconciliation: the analyst's core banking skill
notes.body:
Reconciliation = proving two independent records agree (nostro vs GL, custodian vs internal, trades vs settlements). Breaks come from timing (T+1 settlement), fees, FX, failed posts, and duplicates. The analyst builds the break-report: matched, timing-mismatch, true-break.

Worked example (with solution):
```sql
-- Nostro reconciliation: bank's record vs correspondent's statement.
SELECT COALESCE(b.txn_id, c.txn_id) AS txn_id,
       b.amount AS book_amount, c.amount AS stmt_amount,
       CASE WHEN b.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in books'
            WHEN c.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in statement'
            WHEN b.amount != c.amount THEN 'amount break'
            WHEN b.value_date != c.value_date THEN 'timing break'
            ELSE 'matched' END AS status
FROM book_txns b FULL OUTER JOIN correspondent_stmt c USING (txn_id);
-- Triage order: timing breaks age out; amount breaks get investigated TODAY.
```

notes.title: Custody and asset servicing: holdings, NAV, corporate actions
notes.body:
Custody banks safekeep assets and service them: track holdings, process corporate actions (dividends, splits, mergers), compute NAV (net asset value) for funds. Data challenges: position vs transaction views, ex-dates, and multi-currency valuation.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
NAV computation (simplified):
  NAV = (sum of holding market values + cash + accruals - liabilities) / shares_outstanding
Data traps:
- Corporate action (2:1 split): positions double, price halves; naive
  'holdings changed!' alerts are false — adjust for the action.
- Ex-date: the dividend belongs to holders BEFORE ex-date; settling trades
  across ex-date need special handling.
- FX: value each holding in fund currency at the right rate AND timestamp.
Analyst interview signal: naming ex-dates and corporate-action adjustments
unprompted.
```

notes.title: Regulatory reporting and auditability
notes.body:
Banks report to regulators (call reports, stress tests, AML/KYC filings). Every reported number needs lineage: source system -> transform -> report cell, reproducible on demand. 'Show me how you got this number' is a standing exam, not a surprise audit.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Audit-ready reporting checklist:
1. Lineage: report cell -> mart -> model -> source system (documented).
2. Reproducibility: re-running the pipeline reproduces the number exactly.
3. Controls: four-eyes review on methodology changes; change log.
4. Reconciliation: reported totals tie to the GL.
5. Retention: inputs retained per policy for re-performance.
The analyst's deliverable isn't the number: it's the number PLUS the
proof. Build every report as if the regulator asks tomorrow.
```

notes.title: The reporting chain: subledger to GL to report
notes.body:
Financial reporting flows: source systems -> subledgers -> GL -> reporting marts -> regulatory/internal reports. Each hop transforms and must be provable: completeness (nothing dropped), accuracy (correct values), timeliness (as of the right date). A break anywhere invalidates everything downstream.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Month-end close chain for a lending portfolio:
1. Loan system (source): 48,212 active loans, $4.2B outstanding.
2. Subledger: agrees to source (completeness check: counts + sums).
3. GL: subledger ties to GL control accounts (accuracy check).
4. Mart: mart_daily_lending reconciles to GL (tie-out report).
5. Report: provision number with lineage back to step 1.
If step 4 breaks (mart != GL by $12K): STOP the report, fix the mart,
re-run the tie-out. The report never ships on an untied mart.
```
Independent prep material; no affiliation with or endorsement by BNY Mellon.

notes.title: Reconciliation controls: design and aging
notes.body:
Controls come in flavors: completeness (all records arrived), accuracy (values correct), validity (only authorized records), timeliness (on schedule). Breaks age: day-1 breaks get worked, day-3 breaks escalate, day-5 breaks go to management. An unaged break inventory is a hidden liability.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Break-aging logic for the daily control report:
# age = today - break_date; status in ('open','investigating','escalated','resolved')
# Rules:
#   age >= 5 and status != 'resolved' -> escalate to management
#   amount breaks: investigate same day regardless of age
#   timing breaks: auto-resolve when the lagging leg posts
# The control report shows: total breaks, aged buckets, owner per break.
# An analyst who can't produce the aged inventory can't prove control.
print('Control rule: every break has an owner, an age, and a next action.')
```

notes.title: Change control for reporting logic
notes.body:
Reporting logic changes (new fee rule, new product mapping) go through change control: versioned code, documented rationale, four-eyes review, parallel-run against the old logic, and sign-off. 'I fixed the SQL' without this trail fails every audit.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Change: late-fee logic moves from '30 days' to '25 days' in the provision model.
Control trail:
1. Ticket: CHG-2026-1042 with business rationale + approver.
2. Code: versioned commit, old logic preserved in git history.
3. Review: second analyst reviews the diff (four-eyes).
4. Parallel run: old vs new logic on 3 months; variance explained ($38K).
5. Sign-off: finance owner approves the variance as expected.
6. Deploy: scheduled change window; rollback plan documented.
The parallel-run variance IS the audit evidence.
```

notes.title: Variance analysis: explaining the move
notes.body:
Finance stakeholders ask 'why did X move?' Variance analysis decomposes the change: price vs volume, mix effects, one-timers vs run-rate. The analyst's answer is always a bridge: from last period to this period, naming each driver with its dollar impact.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Provision expense: $1.2M -> $1.7M (+$500K). The bridge:
  +$300K  volume: loan book grew 8% (more exposure, same loss rate)
  +$150K  mix: shift toward higher-risk segments
  +$120K  one-timer: single large commercial default
  -$70K   rate: improved collections in retail book
  =+$500K total (bridge foots to the reported move)
Rule: the bridge must FOOT (sum to the total). An unfooted bridge is
two opinions, not an analysis.
```

notes.title: Speaking finance: tie-outs and sign-off
notes.body:
Finance runs on tie-outs: every number agrees with its independent source before sign-off. The analyst's deliverable package: the number, the tie-out evidence, the variance bridge, and the control report. Sign-off is earned with proof, not asserted with confidence.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Month-end package for the CFO:
1. Headline: provision $1.7M (+$500K MoM).
2. Tie-out: mart total = GL control account (diff $0).
3. Bridge: volume/mix/one-timer/rate decomposition (foots).
4. Controls: break inventory aged; no unresolved amount breaks.
5. Lineage: report cell -> mart -> model -> loan system (one page).
The CFO signs because the package answers every question before it's
asked. Build this package shape for EVERY recurring report.
```

notes.title: The operating rhythm: maker vs manager time
notes.body:
Senior analysts protect deep-work blocks (analysis, modeling) while serving stakeholder time (meetings, ad-hoc). The rhythm: mornings for deep work, afternoons for collaboration, Friday for pipeline health and learning. Context-switching is the tax; batching is the deduction.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sample senior-analyst week:
Mon AM: deep work (the hard analysis) | PM: stakeholder meetings
Tue AM: deep work | PM: pipeline review + code reviews
Wed AM: deep work | PM: metric review prep
Thu: metric review meeting + follow-up analyses
Fri AM: pipeline health + break inventory | PM: learning (new technique)
Rules: no-meeting mornings twice a week (calendar-blocked); ad-hoc requests
triaged, not instantly served ('I'll scope it by 3pm'); the metric review
is sacred (it's where trust compounds).
```

notes.title: The daily/weekly/monthly cadence
notes.body:
Daily: pipeline health check (did everything run? any breaks?), inbox triage, one deep-work block. Weekly: metric review, stakeholder updates, pipeline break inventory. Monthly: deep-dives, roadmap planning, skill investment. The cadence turns chaos into routine.

Worked example (with solution):

2. Freshness: max(event_time) within SLA on critical tables?

```

notes.title: Incident playbook: the dashboard is wrong
notes.body:
Production incidents follow a playbook: acknowledge quickly, assess impact (who sees wrong numbers?), diagnose at pipeline boundaries, communicate status, fix forward, then write the blameless postmortem. Never fix forward silently — the postmortem is where the system improves.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
09:12 Alert: exec dashboard revenue down 40%.
09:15 Acknowledge in #data-ops: 'Investigating; dashboard may show stale data.'
09:25 Diagnose: mart_daily partition for yesterday is EMPTY (load failed at 03:00).
09:30 Communicate: 'Root cause: failed load; rerunning now; ETA 10:30.'
10:25 Rerun completes; quality gates pass; dashboard correct.
10:45 Postmortem: why did the load fail (source schema change)? Add a schema-
drift check as a gate. Action item with owner and date.
Calm, structured, communicative: the senior incident signature.
```

notes.title: Stakeholder portfolio: managing up, down, and across
notes.body:
Senior analysts manage a stakeholder portfolio: executives (decisions, brevity), peers in data eng (contracts, respect), business partners (discovery, reliability), and finance (tie-outs, rigor). Each gets a different cadence and format; all get reliability.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Stakeholder map:
- VP Product: monthly metric review, one-slide decisions, 60-second answers.
- Data Eng: DAG contracts, schema-change notices, blameless postmortems.
- Marketing: weekly office hours (batches ad-hoc into one slot).
- Finance: tie-out packages, variance bridges, audit-ready docs.
The office-hours trick: ad-hoc requests arrive all week but get ANSWERED
in the slot — batching protects deep work while serving partners well.
```

notes.title: Growth: feedback, skills, and compounding habits
notes.body:
Senior growth is deliberate: quarterly feedback (ask 'what should I do more/less of?'), skill investment (one new technique per quarter, applied to real work), teaching (the fastest way to learn), and a portfolio habit (one public artifact per quarter). Careers compound like interest.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Quarterly growth plan:
- Feedback: ask manager + 2 stakeholders the more/less question; write it down.
- Skill: this quarter = dbt testing; apply to the team's marts (real work).
- Teaching: run a 30-min lunch-and-learn on window functions.
- Portfolio: publish the dbt-testing writeup (sanitized) as a blog post.
Each quarter's artifact becomes next quarter's interview story.
The analysts who compound: visible learning, applied immediately, taught
to others, published. That loop is the career.
```

notes.title: The 7-project architecture
notes.body:
Seven projects, each proving a hiring-relevant skill: (1) SQL deep-dive (window functions, CTEs on a real dataset), (2) pandas analysis (wrangling + EDA), (3) statistics/A/B test (experiment analysis with memo), (4) dashboard (BI tool, takeaway-first), (5) Excel model (forecast with checks), (6) domain project (banking/healthcare/retail data story), (7) capstone (end-to-end: question to stakeholder deck). No toy datasets — real, messy, documented.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Project scoping template (fill BEFORE building):

Dataset: e-commerce orders + loyalty table (source + grain documented).
Methods: cohort retention, CAC comparison, Simpson check by tenure.
Deliverable: one-slide recommendation + notebook + dashboard.
Done when: a stranger can reproduce it from the README in 30 minutes.
Build order: SQL (fastest win) -> pandas -> dashboard -> A/B -> Excel ->
domain -> capstone. Early wins fund later motivation.
```

notes.title: What hiring managers actually look for
notes.body:
Hiring managers skim portfolios in minutes. They check: can this person frame a question, handle messiness, choose right methods, communicate a takeaway, and write clean code? They do NOT check: tutorial completion, perfect accuracy, fancy tools. Signal density beats project count.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
90-second README structure (every project):
# Title: the decision question (not 'Sales Analysis')
> One-line takeaway: 'Churn concentrates in month 2; onboarding is the leak.'
## The question | ## Data (source, grain, caveats) | ## Method (3 bullets)
## Key visual (one chart) | ## Recommendation | ## Reproduce (commands)
The hiring manager reads the title + takeaway + visual in 90 seconds
and decides 'interview' or 'pass'. Everything else is for the deep read.
```

notes.title: Real datasets, honestly documented
notes.body:
Use public real datasets (government open data, Kaggle with documented provenance, company-released data) — never fabricate 'real company' data. Document every caveat: sampling, time range, known gaps. Honest limitations are a senior signal; hidden ones are a rejection.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Dataset documentation block (README):
Source: NYC Open Data, taxi trips 2026-01 (link + access date).
Grain: one row per trip. Rows: 2.1M.
Caveats: cash tips underreported; GPS rounding at pickup; Jan only
(seasonality not observable).
License: public domain.
Why this matters: the interviewer WILL ask 'what are this data's limits?'
The documented answer beats the improvised one every time.
```

notes.title: Code quality that survives skimming
notes.body:
Portfolio code is read, not run: clear names, short functions, comments explaining WHY (not what), a requirements file, and deterministic outputs (seeds set). Notebooks: narrative + code, executed top-to-bottom with no hidden state.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Bad: df2 = df[df.x > 5].groupby('y').z.mean()  (what is df2? why 5?)
# Good:
MIN_ORDERS = 5  # filter noise: customers with fewer orders
avg_value_by_segment = (
    customers[customers['orders'] >= MIN_ORDERS]
    .groupby('segment')['lifetime_value'].mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)
# Names say what; the comment says why (filtering noise).
# requirements.txt pins pandas==2.x; random_state=42 everywhere.
```

notes.title: Profile engineering: the 10-second scan
notes.body:
Hiring managers scan your GitHub profile in seconds: pinned repos (your 3 best projects), a profile README (who you are, what you do, links), and visible recent activity. Unpinned tutorial repos and empty profiles signal 'not serious'.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Profile README template:
# Alex Analyst | Data Analyst
> I turn messy data into decisions. SQL, Python, BI.
- Currently: 7-project analytics portfolio (link)
- Ask me about: experimentation, dashboards that get read
- Contact: email | LinkedIn | portfolio site
Pinned: capstone, SQL deep-dive, A/B test analysis (the 3 strongest).
Unpin: course exercises, forks, half-finished experiments.
The profile answers 'who is this and why interview them' in 10 seconds.
```

notes.title: Repo structure that reproduces
notes.body:
Every project repo: README.md (90-second structure), data/ (or download script — never commit huge files), notebooks/ or src/, requirements.txt or environment.yml, and a reproduce script. Git LFS or download scripts handle large data; .gitignore excludes secrets and outputs.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
project-capstone/
  README.md            # 90-second structure
  data/README.md       # 'Download from <link>; 2.1M rows; caveats...'
  notebooks/01_clean.ipynb  # numbered: clean -> eda -> model -> report
  src/reproduce.py     # one command rebuilds all outputs
  requirements.txt     # pinned versions
  .gitignore           # *.csv, .env, outputs/
Reproduce test: git clone -> pip install -r requirements.txt ->
python src/reproduce.py -> outputs match README. 30 minutes max.
```

notes.title: Git hygiene for analysts
notes.body:
Commit messages say what and why ('Add churn cohort analysis; fixes month-2 gap'). Branch for experiments, merge via PR with a summary. Never commit: credentials, raw PII, or 2GB CSVs. The commit history is a work journal interviewers read.

Worked example (with solution):
```bash
# Analyst git workflow:
git checkout -b experiment/loyalty-holdout   # branch per analysis thread
# ... work ...
git add notebooks/03_loyalty.ipynb
# NEVER: git add data/customers_raw.csv  (PII + huge)
git commit -m "Add loyalty holdout analysis: 22% conversion, $41 CAC"
git push origin experiment/loyalty-holdout
# PR description: question, method, finding, caveats -> merge to main
# History reads as a decision journal, not a dump.
```

notes.title: Publishing: Pages, gists, and static exports
notes.body:
Make work clickable: GitHub Pages hosts project sites and dashboards (exported HTML); gists share single-file analyses; nbviewer renders notebooks without cloning. A link the manager can click beats a repo they must clone.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Publishing ladder (easiest first):
1. Rendered notebook via nbviewer link in the README ('view without cloning').
2. Exported dashboard HTML on GitHub Pages (interactive, zero setup).
3. Project microsite on Pages: question, takeaway, key visual, repo link.
4. Blog writeup (the teaching artifact): 'How I found the month-2 churn leak.'
Each rung removes friction between the hiring manager and your best work.
```

notes.title: Contribution habits that compound
notes.body:
Green squares come from real work: weekly project commits, code reviews on your own PRs, issue tracking for analysis tasks. Quality over gaming: one substantive commit beats ten whitespace tweaks. The habit also keeps skills warm between roles.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sustainable contribution rhythm:
- Weekly: one project commit (analysis progress, documented).
- Per project: issues for each analysis question ('#12: Simpson check by tenure').
- PRs with summaries even when solo (the habit transfers to teams).
- Quarterly: one public artifact (blog post, polished project).
What NOT to do: commit-streak gaming, tutorial repos as 'projects',
forking without contributing. Interviewers can tell.
```

notes.title: What makes a dashboard portfolio-grade
notes.body:
Portfolio dashboards prove: chart choice judgment, filter design, takeaway communication, and honest visualization. Three excellent dashboards beat ten mediocre ones. Each needs: the decision question, the takeaway title, comparison context, and documented caveats.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Portfolio dashboard spec (each of the 3):
Decision: 'Should marketing shift spend from paid search to affiliates?'
Takeaway title: 'Affiliates assist 31% of enterprise deals at 1/3 the CAC.'
Visuals: funnel (assisted vs last-click), CAC comparison bar, trend.
Filters: date range, segment (apply consistently, stated in subtitle).
Caveats: attribution window 90 days; affiliate data 2-day lag.
Grain note: 'One row per touchpoint; deduped to opportunity.'
A reviewer learns your judgment from the spec, not just the pixels.
```

notes.title: The hiring-manager dashboard rubric
notes.body:
Reviewers score: (1) Does the title state a takeaway? (2) Is there comparison context? (3) Are filters consistent and purposeful? (4) Are axes honest? (5) Can I state the decision in 30 seconds? Five yeses = portfolio-grade.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Rubric applied to a candidate dashboard:
1. Title 'Churn concentrates in month 2' -> YES (takeaway, not topic).
2. Bars show current vs prior quarter -> YES (comparison).
3. Region filter affects all 4 sheets -> YES (consistent).
4. Bar y-axes start at zero -> YES (honest).
5. 'Fix onboarding month 2' statable in 30s -> YES (decision-clear).
Score 5/5: publish. 3/5: iterate before publishing.
Use this rubric on YOUR OWN dashboards before anyone else does.
```

notes.title: Documenting build decisions
notes.body:
A build-decisions doc (in the repo) records: why this chart, why these filters, the grain, known caveats, and what you'd do with more time. It turns a pretty dashboard into evidence of judgment — and it's the document you walk through in interviews.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
BUILD DECISIONS (dashboard: affiliate ROI):
- Chart: bars not lines for channel comparison (position > angle).
- Filters: date + segment only (the stakeholder's next questions; every
  additional filter was cut as noise).
- Grain: one row per opportunity-touch; deduped on opportunity_id.
- Caveat: 90-day attribution window; affiliate feed lags 2 days.
- With more time: incrementality test to separate correlation from lift.
The last line ('with more time') shows senior self-awareness.
```

notes.title: Publishing dashboards that get clicked
notes.body:
Export to static HTML or publish to a free tier; embed in the project microsite with the decision question above and the takeaway below. Test on mobile (hiring managers browse on phones). Loading time matters: aggregate before publishing, not in the browser.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Publishing checklist:
- Exported HTML < 5MB (aggregated data, not row-level).
- Decision question as the page H1; takeaway as the subhead.
- Tested on a phone: titles readable, filters tappable.
- Caveats in a visible footnote (not buried).
- Link from the repo README + the portfolio microsite.
A dashboard nobody can open might as well not exist.
```

notes.title: Iterating: the critique cycle
notes.body:
Portfolio dashboards improve through critique cycles: self-review against the rubric, peer review (trade with another analyst), and the 30-second test with a non-analyst. Each cycle fixes one class of issues; three cycles is usually enough.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Critique cycle log:
Cycle 1 (self): titles were topics -> rewrote as takeaways.
Cycle 2 (peer): filters affected 3 of 5 sheets -> made consistent.
Cycle 3 (non-analyst friend): 'What am I supposed to decide?' -> added
  the decision question as H1 and a recommendation callout.
Document the cycles in the repo: the iteration log IS the growth story
interviewers love ('show me how you improved something').
```
