notes.title: Capstone scoping: the one-page brief
notes.body:
The capstone brief fits one page: the decision, why it matters (dollars), the data (sources, grain, access), the methods, the risks (what could kill it), and the timeline with milestones. If the brief doesn't fit one page, the scope is wrong.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
CAPSTONE BRIEF: Should Northwind expand its loyalty program?
Why it matters: loyalty members are 18% of customers, 34% of revenue.
Data: orders (2.1M rows, grain: line item), loyalty table, marketing spend.
Methods: cohort retention, CAC comparison, Simpson check by tenure,
  sensitivity analysis on attribution window.
Risks: loyalty table has 12% dup keys (dedup plan); attribution is
  correlational (holdout recommended, not claimed).
Timeline: W1 scope+data, W2 SQL/pandas, W3 stats+viz, W4 report+deck.
Done when: 10-min walkthrough + reproducible repo + stakeholder deck.
```

notes.title: Execution: the full stack in four weeks
notes.body:
Week 1: scope + data audit (profile everything, document caveats). Week 2: SQL + pandas analysis (answer the question three ways, reconcile). Week 3: statistics + visualization (CIs, segments, takeaway-first charts). Week 4: report + deck + walkthrough rehearsal. Each week ends with a reviewable artifact.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Week 2 reconciliation (the senior habit):
  SQL:    loyalty revenue share = 34.2%
  pandas: loyalty revenue share = 34.2%
  Excel spot-check (100-row sample): 34% (rounding)
All three agree -> the number is real. If they disagreed, the DEFINITIONS
differ (filters, NULLs, dups): reconcile before proceeding.
Week 3 Simpson check: loyalty lift holds within tenure bands (not a mix
artifact). Week 4: the deck leads with the recommendation.
The capstone is 4 reconciled weeks, not 4 weeks of hoping.
```

notes.title: The report: structure that persuades
notes.body:
Capstone report structure: executive summary (decision + takeaway + recommendation, one page), question & data (with caveats), methods (just enough to trust), findings (takeaway-first visuals), risks & limits, recommendation, appendix (reproducibility). Write the executive summary LAST.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (one page):
Decision: expand loyalty? Recommendation: 90-day holdout in 3 regions,
  not full rollout.
Takeaway: members retain 2x, but the lift concentrates in tenured users;
  marginal members cost $41 CAC vs $18 for the core.
Evidence: cohort chart, CAC bridge, Simpson-checked segments.
Risk: attribution is correlational; the holdout measures true lift.
Ask: approve the holdout ($120K test budget).
A executive reads this page and decides. Everything else is due diligence.
```

notes.title: The 10-minute walkthrough: rehearsed, not read
notes.body:
The walkthrough is a performance: 10 minutes, no reading slides, every visual introduced by its takeaway. Rehearse with a timer; plant the 3 questions you'll get (data limits, method choice, 'what would you do differently') and answer them before they're asked.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Walkthrough beats (rehearsed):
0:00 The decision + my recommendation (up front).
1:30 The data: 3 tables, grain, the 12% dup-key fix (messiness handled).
3:30 Method in 3 bullets (cohorts, CAC, Simpson check).
5:30 Findings: 2 visuals, takeaways stated before showing.
7:30 Risks: correlational attribution -> holdout recommendation (honesty).
9:00 The ask: approve the $120K test.
9:30 Buffer for questions.
Rehearse 5x with a timer. Record once; watch for filler words and
'so basically' hedging. The walkthrough is the interview.
```

notes.title: Pre-mortem and reproducibility audit
notes.body:
Pre-mortem: 'It's six months later and the capstone failed. Why?' List the failure modes (data went stale, method was wrong, recommendation ignored) and harden against them now. Reproducibility audit: fresh clone, follow README, verify every number.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Pre-mortem (capstone):
- 'The loyalty table refreshed with a new schema; my queries broke.'
  -> Harden: schema-check gate in the reproduce script.
- 'An interviewer found the Simpson problem I missed.'
  -> Harden: segment every finding by the top 2 confounders NOW.
- 'Nobody could reproduce it.'
  -> Harden: the 30-minute stranger test before calling it done.
Reproducibility audit: new machine, clone, pip install, run, diff outputs
vs README. Every mismatch fixed, not explained away.
Done = brief + 4 weeks + report + walkthrough + pre-mortem + audit.
```

notes.title: The loop, stage by stage
notes.body:
Typical senior analyst loop: recruiter screen (background, comp expectations), hiring-manager screen (scope fit), technical rounds (SQL live, stats/probability, take-home or case), behavioral (STAR stories), final (presentation or panel). Each stage filters differently; prepare per stage, not generically.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Stage-by-stage prep:
Recruiter (15-30 min): 2-min pitch, comp range researched, 3 questions.
Hiring manager (45 min): scope stories (stakeholders, decisions influenced).
SQL live (45-60 min): narrate-first; the 6-pattern drill set.
Stats/probability (45 min): Bayes, CIs, A/B design from this course.
Case/take-home (3-5 hrs): capstone walkthrough format.
Behavioral (45 min): 5 STAR stories with numbers.
Final/panel: 10-min capstone walkthrough + Q&A.
One generic prep fails all stages; stage-specific prep passes each.
```

notes.title: The technical question bank
notes.body:
SQL: top-N per group, funnel, streaks, MoM, dedup, anti-join (this course's drills). Stats: Bayes with base rates, CI interpretation, A/B design, Simpson's paradox. Product: metric design, trade-offs, estimation. Behavioral: disagreement, failure, influence, mentoring, ambiguity.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Two-week technical sprint (1 hr/day):
Days 1-3: SQL patterns (2/day, narrated, timed).
Days 4-5: probability (Bayes + counting, with closers).
Days 6-7: A/B design (write 3 experiment plans).
Days 8-9: product sense (metric design for 2 products).
Day 10: estimation (3 Fermi problems, structured).
Days 11-12: behavioral stories (write + rehearse 5 STARs).
Days 13-14: full mock loop (below).
Sprint output: a personal 'miss log' driving the next sprint.
```

notes.title: Mock loops: realistic conditions
notes.body:
Mocks must simulate pressure: timed, camera on, stranger interviewer (peer swap), no pausing. Record; review against a rubric (correctness, narration, edge cases, communication). One mock per week during active search; the miss log becomes the drill list.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Mock rubric (score 1-5 each):
- Correctness: right answer, verified.
- Narration: restated, grain stated, thinking aloud.
- Edge cases: NULLs, dups, ties, timezones named.
- Communication: takeaway-first, no rambling.
- Poise: handled the follow-up without flustering.
After: top 2 misses -> 20-min drills each, re-mock in 3 days.
The loop that improves: mock -> rubric -> drills -> re-mock.
Mocks without rubrics are just anxiety practice.
```

notes.title: Take-homes and case presentations
notes.body:
Take-homes test judgment under realistic conditions: scope the question, document assumptions, show method, state takeaways, note limits. Timebox ruthlessly (the stated hours, not 3x). The presentation: 10-minute walkthrough + Q&A; they probe choices, not polish.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Take-home rules:
1. Read twice; restate the decision in your own words (in the doc).
2. Assumptions section FIRST (they grade your judgment here).
3. Method: 3 bullets, not a textbook.
4. Takeaway-first visuals; caveats visible.
5. 'With more time' section (scope awareness).
6. Ship at the timebox: completeness within limits beats perfection late.
Presentation: the capstone walkthrough format. Q&A prep: for every
choice, know the alternative you rejected and why.
```

notes.title: Offers and negotiation
notes.body:
Evaluate offers on: total comp (base + bonus + equity, annualized), scope (team, decisions, data access), manager (your growth lever), and trajectory (what the next role looks like). Negotiate with competing timelines honestly; never fabricate competing offers.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Offer evaluation sheet:
- Base / bonus target / equity (4-yr, vesting) -> annualized total.
- Scope: team size, stakeholder level, decision rights.
- Manager: 1:1 cadence? growth track record?
- Trajectory: what does promotion look like in 18 months?
- Logistics: remote/hybrid, hours expectations.
Negotiation script: 'I'm excited about the scope. Based on [market data
+ competing timeline], I was targeting [range]. Is there flexibility?'
One round, honest, data-backed. Then decide and commit fully.
```

objectives: Build a 90-day plan integrating certification study, portfolio completion, and job applications.
Sequence certifications by ROI: which to take, in what order, and when to stop certifying and start applying.
Run a job-search pipeline: targeting, tailoring, tracking, and follow-up with weekly metrics.
Maintain momentum: routines, accountability, and burnout guards for a sustained search.

notes.title: The 90-day architecture
notes.body:
90 days, three phases: Days 1-30 (skill sprints + portfolio projects 1-3 + cert #1 study), Days 31-60 (portfolio 4-6 + cert #1 exam + applications begin), Days 61-90 (capstone + cert #2 + full application pipeline + interviews). Certifications and portfolio interleave; applications start when proof exists, not before.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Week-by-week (10 hrs/day full-time search):
W1-2:  SQL sprint + portfolio P1 (SQL deep-dive) + Google cert courses 1-2
W3-4:  pandas sprint + P2 + cert courses 3-4
W5-6:  stats/A-B sprint + P3 + cert courses 5-6; EXAM Google cert
W7-8:  BI sprint + P4 (dashboard) + PL-300 study begins; 5 apps/week start
W9-10: Excel + P5; PL-300 exam; 10 apps/week
W11:   Domain project P6; interview prep sprint begins
W12:   Capstone + 15 apps/week + mock loops
Adjust hours to your reality; the SEQUENCE is what matters.
```

notes.title: Certification ROI: which, when, when to stop
notes.body:
Certifications have diminishing returns: the first proves baseline, the second adds a specialty, the third is procrastination. ROI order for analysts: one broad (Google DA), one tool-depth (PL-300 or Tableau), then STOP and let the portfolio + interviews carry. Never certify instead of applying.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Cert decision matrix:
Google Data Analytics: broad baseline, portfolio-friendly -> FIRST.
PL-300: Power BI depth for BI-heavy roles -> SECOND (if targeting BI roles).
Tableau Certified: viz depth -> SECOND (if targeting Tableau shops).
Data+: vendor-neutral breadth -> alternative first cert.
STOP rule: after 2 certs, every additional study hour goes to applications
and interview prep. The third cert's marginal interview value ~= 0.
Exam-day: sleep > cramming; scenario questions reward rested judgment.
```

notes.title: The application pipeline
notes.body:
Treat applications as a pipeline: target list (20-30 companies, researched), tailored resume per role (mirror the posting's language), portfolio link in every application, tracking spreadsheet (company, role, date, stage, follow-up), and follow-up cadence (7 days, then 21).

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Pipeline metrics (weekly review):
- Applications sent: 10-15/week (quality > spray).
- Response rate: target 15-25% (below 10%: fix resume/portfolio).
- Screen -> technical: target 50% (below: drill the weak stage).
- Technical -> final: target 30%.
- Offer rate per final: 25-35%.
Funnel math: 12 apps/week x 12 weeks = 144 apps -> ~25 screens ->
~12 technicals -> ~4 finals -> ~1-2 offers. Work the funnel, not luck.
Tailoring: 20 min per application (mirror posting language, reorder bullets).
```

notes.title: Interview prep integration
notes.body:
Prep integrates with the pipeline: SQL drills daily (15 min), one mock per week once screens start, STAR stories written before the first interview, capstone walkthrough rehearsed before finals. Prep without pipeline is rehearsal without a stage; pipeline without prep wastes opportunities.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Weekly rhythm (active search):
Mon-Fri: 15-min SQL drill (morning) + applications (2-3/day).
Wed: 1-hr stats/probability review (rotate topics).
Sat: mock loop (alternating: SQL live / case / behavioral).
Sun: miss-log review + drill plan for the week.
The 15-min daily drill compounds: 90 days x 15 min = 22 hours of SQL
fluency. Consistency beats cramming; the miss log aims the work.
```

notes.title: Momentum: routines and burnout guards
notes.body:
A 90-day search is a marathon: fixed work hours, one full day off weekly, exercise, and a weekly review (metrics + feelings). Burnout signals: dreading applications, doomscrolling instead of drills, skipping mocks. The fix is structural (rest, smaller batches), not motivational.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sustainable search rules:
- Work 9-5 on the search; evenings are yours (no 'one more application').
- One full day off per week (recovery is productive).
- Weekly review: pipeline metrics + energy check (1-5).
- Accountability: one partner for weekly check-ins (or this course's plan).
- Rejection protocol: log it, extract one lesson, next application within 24h.
Rejections are funnel data, not verdicts: 144 apps -> 1-2 offers means
~142 rejections are the PLAN working, not failing.
```
